lessons.title: Before changing the IR
lessons.summary: Recall SSA and dominance, learn the memory operations we will introduce, and locate the exact boundary between inspection and transformation.
lessons.takeaway: Changing IR means taking responsibility for both its structure and behavior.

blocks.text: Task: Read this context before editing FlatteningPass. Day 1 built the plugin, statistics, CFG analysis, and eligibility checker. Day 2 starts changing eligible functions.
What are we trying to build?

A dispatcher is a block that reads a state number and uses a switch to choose the next program block. Eventually, an original branch will become “store the destination state, then branch to the dispatcher.” We have not implemented that complete transformation yet.

original entry/setup → dispatcher → selected original block
                           ↑                  |
                           └──────────────────┘
The original entry stays a one-time setup block. Its stack slots must not be allocated repeatedly in the dispatcher. Return and unreachable blocks finish their path instead of looping back.
Recall SSA and dominance

An SSA value has one definition. That definition must dominate its uses: every reachable path from entry to a use passes through the definition. Adding dispatcher edges can create new paths that violate that relationship, even if the original program never had a problem.
The memory operations you will see

rows: Allocate space for one i32 in the current function’s stack frame; the result is a pointer.
Write %x into the storage addressed by %slot; the instruction produces no result.
Read an i32 from that address; the result is a new SSA value.
Select an incoming value according to the predecessor edge used to enter the block.

blocks.text: Demotion replaces selected SSA dependencies with stores and loads. “Register” here means an LLVM SSA, register-like value—not a guaranteed physical CPU register. The original arithmetic remains; the way its result reaches users changes.
Your starting template
Edit the existing lib/FlatteningPass.cpp. Do not create a second run() definition. The eligibility guard from Day 1 stays at the top; every new mutation belongs after it.
How to use the lessons

items: Start with the template. Fill in each numbered step yourself.
Use the full implementation to compare only after trying the exercise. Snippets state where to insert them.
Run verify after each complete structural change. It checks valid IR, not equivalent program behavior.
A template containing TODOs is an exercise scaffold, not a claim that the transformation is finished.

blocks.text: Checkpoint: Why must eligibility run before mutation? Why is a successful verifier run weaker than proving that a transformation preserves behavior?

quiz.q: Why prepare SSA values before adding dispatcher edges?
choices: Extra edges can break definition-to-use dominance
The verifier requires every function to use memory
PHIs are forbidden in all LLVM programs
quiz.why: PHIs are valid LLVM IR. It is our planned CFG restructuring that can invalidate existing SSA relationships.

lessons.title: Collect PHIs without changing them
lessons.summary: Build a small worklist of PHI pointers, using mutable traversal and a checked downcast. Verify the count before introducing mutation.

blocks.text: Task: Collect PHI nodes in the existing FlatteningPass::run(), after the eligibility guard. This lesson does not modify IR.
The template to start with
Step 1 — Include the types and container
Instructions.h defines PHINode and other instruction subclasses. Casting.h supplies LLVM’s type checks. std::vector is a growable collection; this vector’s element type is PHINode*, not Instruction*.
Step 2 — Traverse existing instructions by reference

F is a mutable Function&. Therefore auto &BB and auto &I refer to mutable existing blocks and instructions. Plain auto would try to copy objects; const auto & would prevent collecting the mutable PHI pointers needed by the later utility.
Step 3 — Keep the result of dyn_cast

dyn_cast returns a PHINode* when the instruction is a PHI, or nullptr otherwise. The if tests that pointer. push_back copies the pointer into the vector; it does not copy or take ownership of the instruction.
Step 4 — Print and preserve
llvm::errs() << "Number of PHIs: " << phis.size() << "\n";
Keep PreservedAnalyses::all(): collecting pointers and printing a count leave IR unchanged. The existing function declaration and rejection returns also remain unchanged.
The full implementation of this insertion
Verify

cmake --build build
opt -load-pass-plugin="$PWD/build/libMiniShield.so" \
  -passes='function(minishield-flatten),verify' \
  -disable-output tests/ir/phi.ll
Checkpoint: What does the vector own? Why do we retain pointers rather than copies? What changes when a later utility deletes a PHI?

choices: The entire PHI instruction
Only the pointer value
The function containing the PHI
quiz.why: LLVM owns the instruction. The vector keeps its address so a later pass stage can find it.

lessons.title: Keep the typed pointer from dyn_cast
lessons.originalTitle: Keep the typed pointer from dyn_cast
lessons.summary: Understand the actual push_back error: a successful type test does not change the declared type of the original instruction.
lessons.takeaway: A type check is useful only if you keep the typed result you need.

blocks.text: Task: Fix the pointer-type mismatch encountered while collecting PHIs. Work in the inner instruction loop from the previous lesson.
The failing template
Step 1 — Read the declared types

A PHINode derives from Instruction. Converting PHINode* to Instruction* is an upcast. The reverse needs a check: an arbitrary Instruction* might identify an add, branch, load, or return. A condition does not automatically narrow the C++ type of I.
Step 2 — Name the cast result
auto *phi = llvm::dyn_cast<llvm::PHINode>(&I);
This does not allocate a PHI. It gives a more specific pointer to the same instruction if the type matches. The draft discarded this pointer and then pushed the original, less-specific &I.
Step 3 — Append only a successful cast
Use an if-initializer-style declaration in the condition so the typed pointer is available inside the body. A null pointer skips the body.
The full corrected fragment
Observed error: phis.push_back(&I) fails because the vector needs PHINode* but &I remains Instruction*. Saving the result as phi makes the argument type match.
Verify

cmake --build build
opt -load-pass-plugin="$PWD/build/libMiniShield.so" \
  -passes='function(minishield-flatten),verify' \
  -disable-output tests/ir/phi.ll
Compilation should succeed and the phi.ll count should still be 1. We have changed C++ bookkeeping, not LLVM IR.
Checkpoint: Why is &I later valid for a vector<Instruction*> but invalid here? Explain the difference between a runtime type test and the static type of an expression.

quiz.q: Does a successful dyn_cast used only as an if condition retype I?
choices: Yes, I becomes a PHINode reference
No; keep the returned PHINode pointer
Yes, but only inside the if body
quiz.why: I keeps its declared type. The returned pointer is the value with the more specific type.

lessons.title: Demote PHIs after collection
lessons.summary: Use LLVM’s per-PHI utility, understand why it must run after traversal, and recognize the changed IR and analysis-preservation decision.
lessons.takeaway: The PHI disappears; incoming paths store and users load.

blocks.text: Task: After collecting PHIs, replace each PHI with stack-based data flow. This is the first lesson that actually changes the program’s IR.
The template to start with
Step 1 — Include the transformation helper
#include "llvm/Transforms/Utils/Local.h"

The installed LLVM 23 API is a free function: DemotePHIToStack(PHINode*, optional insertion point). There is no DemotePHIToStack::runOnFunction(F) method. The default insertion behavior is enough for these study fixtures.
Step 2 — Process the saved pointers
llvm::DemotePHIToStack(phi);

The utility allocates stack storage, arranges stores of incoming values and loads for users, and deletes the PHI. Do not dereference phi after this call. The vector still contains that address, but the instruction it identified no longer exists.
Step 3 — Invalidate after a change

Return PreservedAnalyses::none() after demotion. Return all() if there were no PHIs and nothing changed. This early return is correct for this PHI-only checkpoint; a later lesson removes it when a second transformation stage must run even without PHIs.
The full implementation of this stage
Verify

cmake --build build
opt -load-pass-plugin="$PWD/build/libMiniShield.so" \
  -passes='function(minishield-flatten),verify' \
  -S tests/ir/phi.ll -o build/phi-demoted.ll
cat build/phi-demoted.ll
Expected data flow

entry:  allocate %value.slot once
left:   store 10 into %value.slot
right:  store 20 into %value.slot
join:   load %value.slot and return the loaded value
Expect no PHI instruction, one slot for this PHI, stores in left and right, and a load for the return in join. Actual generated names can differ. The original branch structure remains.
Observed error: Do not delete PHIs while using an ordinary loop over the same instruction list. Collecting first avoids using an invalidated iterator.
Checkpoint: Trace both outcomes of the condition. Which store executes? What does join load? Why must changing IR invalidate cached analyses?

quiz.q: Why collect PHIs before demoting them?
choices: The utility deletes the PHI and can invalidate ordinary traversal
A vector is required by the LLVM API
PHIs have no operands until put into a vector
quiz.why: Demotion mutates the instruction list. A worklist separates discovery from deletion.

lessons.title: Find values that cross block boundaries
lessons.originalTitle: Find values that cross block boundaries
lessons.summary: PHI demotion can introduce a load whose result is still used in other blocks. Find those definitions before changing the CFG.
lessons.takeaway: No PHIs does not mean no cross-block SSA dependencies.

blocks.text: Task: After PHI demotion, collect remaining instruction results used outside their defining block. Do not demote this new collection yet.
Before you begin — definition versus use

header:
  %i.reload = load i32, ptr %i.reg2mem
  ; ...
body:
  %next = add i32 %i.reload, 1
exit:
  ret i32 %i.reload

The load defines i.reload in header, while body and exit use it. That is a cross-block dependency. The current CFG makes header dominate those uses. A dispatcher can add a path that bypasses header, so the dependency needs preparation.
The template to start with
Step 1 — Use the right vector element type

This worklist may contain loads, arithmetic, or other value-producing instructions. Use Instruction*, the common base type, rather than PHINode*. Function arguments and constants are not instructions in these block lists; they are not collected here.
Step 2 — Filter unsuitable candidates

if (I.getType()->isVoidTy() || llvm::isa<llvm::AllocaInst>(I))
    continue;

A void instruction has no result to spill. The alloca is the storage object itself and is excluded in this exercise. Lessons 05 and 06 explain both tests. This is the study-fixture preparation policy, not a claim that every possible allocation or instruction type is supported by the final flattener.
Step 3 — Test where the result is used

if (I.isUsedOutsideOfBlock(&BB))
    escapingValues.push_back(&I);

The method is called on the defining instruction and asks whether its result is used outside BB. Here &I has exactly the vector’s Instruction* element type. Only record pointers during this traversal.
Step 4 — Inspect the collection

for (const auto *value : escapingValues)
    llvm::errs() << "cross-block value: " << value->getName() << "\n";

Remove the old PHI-empty early return so this stage is reached even without PHIs; lesson 07 explains the change-tracking detail. LLVM values need not have names, so these names are a learning diagnostic rather than a general test interface.
The full collection fragment
Verify

cmake --build build
opt -load-pass-plugin="$PWD/build/libMiniShield.so" \
  -passes='function(minishield-flatten),verify' \
  -disable-output tests/ir/loop.ll
After PHI demotion in the current loop fixture, expect i.reload in the worklist. Merely creating the new collection changes no IR; PHI demotion may already have changed it.
Checkpoint: Find the defining instruction and a use in a different block. Why does a fresh traversal have to happen after PHI demotion rather than before it?

quiz.q: Why can a PHI-free function still need preparation?
choices: Ordinary instruction results can be used in other blocks
All PHI-free functions contain invalid IR
A PHI-free function cannot contain loads
quiz.why: SSA dependencies are not limited to PHIs. A load or add defined in one block can be consumed in another.

lessons.title: Ask whether an instruction produces a value
lessons.originalTitle: Ask whether an instruction produces a value
lessons.summary: Distinguish an instruction’s result type from its operands and from the function’s return type.
lessons.takeaway: ret i32 returns from the function, but the ret instruction itself has no result.

blocks.text: Task: Fill in the void-result filter inside the inner instruction loop. This prevents collecting operations that produce no value.
The template to start with
Step 1 — Ask the instruction for its result type
I.getType()
This returns an llvm::Type*. It describes the value produced by this instruction, not the type of its first operand. Use -> to call a method on that type pointer.
Step 2 — Test the type
I.getType()->isVoidTy()
void means the instruction does not produce a value for another instruction to use. The name isVoidTy is an LLVM type predicate; it returns a boolean.
Step 3 — Skip this inner-loop iteration

if (I.getType()->isVoidTy())
    continue;
continue advances to the next instruction. It does not return from run(), skip the rest of the function, or mark the IR changed.
Read these examples
In ret i32 %x, i32 is the type of the value returned by the function. The ret instruction itself produces no SSA result. There is no %new = ret ... value for later instructions to consume.
The full filter

if (I.getType()->isVoidTy())
    continue;
Verify

Rebuild and inspect loop.ll’s collection. Its stores, branches, and return should not enter escapingValues. Its load can still be a candidate. The alloca is not void, so it needs the next lesson’s separate filter.
Checkpoint: Why does ret i32 %x have void instruction type? Why does checking I.getOperand(0)->getType() answer a different question?

quiz.q: What is the result type of the instruction ret i32 %x?
choices: i32, because the function returns an integer
void, because the instruction produces no SSA result
ptr, because it transfers control
quiz.why: The returned operand has type i32. The ret instruction itself has no result.

lessons.title: Recognize the stack allocation itself
lessons.summary: Use isa when you only need a yes/no answer. Understand why alloca survives the void filter.
lessons.takeaway: The storage pointer is not the value we are trying to spill into storage.

blocks.text: Task: Add an AllocaInst filter alongside the void-result filter. Keep the worklist focused on values to demote, not their storage allocations.
The template to start with

if (I.getType()->isVoidTy() || /* TODO: recognize alloca */)
    continue;
Step 1 — Recall what alloca returns
%slot = alloca i32
This allocates space for an i32 and returns a pointer to that space. The result type is ptr, not i32 and not void. Consequently isVoidTy() does not exclude it.
Step 2 — Use a type predicate
llvm::isa<llvm::AllocaInst>(I)
isa<T> returns whether the instruction belongs to that class. We only need to skip the instruction; we do not need an AllocaInst* or any alloca-specific methods. Therefore isa is enough.
Step 3 — Combine the filters
The || operator means either condition is sufficient. Short-circuit evaluation stops after a true first condition, though both checks here are read-only.
The full filter

if (I.getType()->isVoidTy() || llvm::isa<llvm::AllocaInst>(I))
    continue;
isa versus dyn_cast

rows: Recognize an alloca to skip it.
Collect a PHINode* or inspect intrinsic-specific information.

blocks.text: Keep stack slots in the actual entry/setup block when designing the dispatcher. Excluding allocas from this worklist does not make arbitrary non-entry or dynamic allocations automatically safe to flatten.
Verify
Rebuild and inspect the cross-block worklist for the demoted loop. The slot pointer crosses blocks, but the allocation should not appear in escapingValues. The i.reload instruction result should.
Checkpoint: Why would skipping only void instructions leave alloca in consideration? When would you choose dyn_cast instead of isa?

quiz.q: Why does the alloca instruction need a separate filter?
choices: It returns a pointer, so it is not void
It is a function declaration
It is never represented as an LLVM instruction
quiz.why: The allocated element is i32, but the allocation instruction’s result is a pointer to that storage.

lessons.title: Finish collection without a premature return
lessons.originalTitle: Finish collection without a premature return
lessons.summary: Review the two missing pieces found in the draft: appending candidates and reaching this stage when the PHI list is empty.
lessons.takeaway: Zero PHIs does not imply unchanged IR or no remaining work.

blocks.text: Task: Review the complete preparation flow so every eligible function reaches cross-block inspection.
The template to start with
Step 1 — Remove the old early return

A PHI-only transformation could stop immediately when its PHI worklist was empty. The expanded pipeline cannot: a PHI-free function can still have an add used in another block. An empty range naturally performs zero iterations, so the PHI loop needs no special guard.
Step 2 — Actually append candidates

Observed error: The reviewed draft created escapingValues and applied the filters, but did not push any instruction. A filter rejects unsuitable values; it does not automatically collect the suitable ones.
Step 3 — Report only real mutation

This is the end of a collection-only checkpoint: only PHI demotion has modified IR so far. The next mutation stage will add escapingValues to this decision. Querying phis.empty() is safe even after the instructions were deleted; do not dereference their stored pointers.
The full insertion after PHI collection
Verify the path with no PHIs
Write tests/ir/cross-block.ll. This test isolates the early-return problem without involving a PHI:

define i32 @cross_block(i32 %x) {
entry:
  %sum = add i32 %x, 1
  br label %exit
exit:
  ret i32 %sum
}
Run the flattening pass with verify. Expect zero PHIs but sum in escapingValues. The fixture is an exercise to write; a reference snippet in this book does not create the file for you.
Checkpoint: Why is &I the right type for this vector but not the PHI vector? Why must success in the eligibility checker and preservation information remain separate decisions?

quiz.q: At the collection-only checkpoint, does a nonempty escapingValues list itself mean IR changed?
choices: Yes, collecting a pointer modifies the instruction
No; only transformations, such as the PHI demotion already performed, change IR
Yes, but only for named instructions
quiz.why: The worklist is C++ bookkeeping. Update changed when a transformation runs, not merely because a candidate was found.

lessons.title: Read the demotion helper signatures
lessons.summary: Compare pointer and reference parameters before calling the next utility. Understand the return value, default arguments, and what the worklist does not own.
lessons.takeaway: Pass the type the function declares, not the type you happen to store.

blocks.text: Task: Read both helper declarations in llvm/Transforms/Utils/Local.h before adding the next call.
The template to complete
Step 1 — Compare the first parameters
These lines explain the API shape; the comments stand for optional parameters, so they are not a replacement header to paste into your source. The real functions are already declared by Local.h.
Step 2 — Dereference the stored pointer
llvm::DemoteRegToStack(*value);

value is Instruction*. The expression *value refers to the existing Instruction object, matching Instruction&. This does not copy the instruction. Contrast DemotePHIToStack(phi), whose parameter is already a pointer.
Step 3 — Understand the result

Both helpers return a pointer to the created stack allocation. The current exercise can ignore that pointer. The function’s IR owns the inserted allocation; ignoring the return value does not delete it.
The full call loop
Verify before integrating

Read the actual declarations in the installed LLVM headers. DemoteRegToStack also has optional parameters, including whether loads are volatile and an allocation insertion point. The study fixtures use the defaults; do not invent a runOnFunction method.
Checkpoint: Explain what *value does here, why phi previously needed no dereference, and why the vector is a worklist rather than an owner of LLVM instructions.

quiz.q: escapingValues stores Instruction*. What does the first DemoteRegToStack parameter require?
choices: An Instruction&, supplied by *value
An Instruction**, supplied by &value
A copy of the whole Function
quiz.why: Dereferencing the stored pointer supplies the existing instruction as a reference, matching the signature.

lessons.title: Demote the escaping values
lessons.summary: Complete the second mutation stage, preserve the collect-then-transform order, and test a function with no PHIs.
lessons.takeaway: Mutation tracking must account for both transformation stages.

blocks.text: Task: Add cross-block value demotion after escapingValues collection. The eligibility guard still runs before either transformation.
The template to start with
Step 1 — Transform only after collection ends

for (auto *value : escapingValues)
    llvm::DemoteRegToStack(*value);

The helper adds an allocation, a store of the computed result, and loads for its uses. The defining calculation remains. Do not insert and rewrite instructions while discovering candidates with an ordinary traversal.
Step 2 — Combine the change conditions
const bool changed = !phis.empty() || !escapingValues.empty();
A function with zero PHIs can still be transformed by the second loop. Preserving analyses in that case would leave stale cached results available to later passes.
The full preparation stage
Use this after the eligibility guard. Replace the earlier preparation and final return; do not paste a second copy of those loops below it.
Verify the loop fixture

cmake --build build
opt -load-pass-plugin="$PWD/build/libMiniShield.so" \
  -passes='function(minishield-flatten),verify' \
  -S tests/ir/loop.ll -o build/loop-demoted.ll
cat build/loop-demoted.ll

Expect no PHIs and additional stack operations. The header stores the former i.reload result into its own slot; body and exit load that slot instead of directly using a header-defined SSA result. Exact names and load counts can vary.
Verify the no-PHI path
Run the same command on the cross-block.ll exercise from lesson 07. Even with zero PHIs, sum should be stored into a slot and exit should return a load from it. Keep generated IR under build/.
Checkpoint: Which transformation ran if phis is empty but escapingValues is not? Why must the final preservation result be none() in that case?

quiz.q: What happens to the original add instruction after DemoteRegToStack?
choices: It is replaced by a PHI
It remains; its result is stored and uses become loads
It moves into the C++ vector
quiz.why: Ordinary-value demotion keeps the computation and changes how its result reaches users.

lessons.title: Trace ordinary-value demotion
lessons.summary: Follow the same result from an add through a store and load. Separate the C++ worklist from the LLVM stack slot it helps create.
lessons.takeaway: The computation stays; the route from definition to consumer changes.

blocks.text: Task: Trace the cross-block example by hand, then compare its generated IR. This is a reading exercise, not another transformation to add.
The input to start with

define i32 @cross_block(i32 %x) {
entry:
  %sum = add i32 %x, 1
  br label %exit
exit:
  ret i32 %sum
}
The template to fill in

entry:
  %sum.slot = alloca i32
  %sum = add i32 %x, 1
  ; TODO: store the computed value before leaving entry.
  br label %exit
exit:
  ; TODO: load the saved value and return that load.
Step 1 — Keep the calculation
The add still computes x+1. We are not replacing arithmetic with a different algorithm. “Demote” changes how the SSA result is carried between blocks.
Step 2 — Store after definition
store i32 %sum, ptr %sum.slot
The value operand and the pointed-to storage are different things. sum is an i32 result; sum.slot is a pointer. The store instruction itself has void type.
Step 3 — Load where the consumer needs the value

%sum.loaded = load i32, ptr %sum.slot
ret i32 %sum.loaded
The return now uses a value defined by a load in its own block. The allocation pointer still crosses blocks, so keep its allocation in the true entry block that dominates these accesses.
The full conceptual result

define i32 @cross_block(i32 %x) {
entry:
  %sum.slot = alloca i32
  %sum = add i32 %x, 1
  store i32 %sum, ptr %sum.slot
  br label %exit
exit:
  %sum.loaded = load i32, ptr %sum.slot
  ret i32 %sum.loaded
}
This is illustrative IR. LLVM’s generated names may differ. For x=4, the add computes 5, the store writes 5, and the load supplies 5 to the return.
What the vector does
escapingValues is a C++ worklist of instruction pointers. DemoteRegToStack rewrites the IR those pointers identify; it does not convert the C++ vector into a stack slot.
Verify

Generate cross-block.ll’s output with the pass followed by verify. Locate the add, its store, the slot allocation, and the load used by the return. A valid result alone is not proof that every future dispatcher preserves the store-before-load order.
Checkpoint: For x=4, what is stored and what is returned? Which object is the pointer, which is the i32, and which is just C++ bookkeeping?

quiz.q: Does the alloca result contain the saved integer directly?
choices: No, it is a pointer to storage that the store writes
Yes, alloca i32 returns an i32
Only when it is stored in escapingValues
quiz.why: The integer is written into the allocated memory. The SSA result of alloca is the address of that memory.

lessons.title: Trace PHI demotion by predecessor
lessons.summary: See how stores on incoming paths replace predecessor-based selection. Compare it directly with ordinary instruction demotion.
lessons.takeaway: A PHI disappears; the path taken determines which store supplies its former users.

blocks.text: Task: Trace the phi.ll diamond on both paths. Do not add a second demotion loop—this lesson explains the utility already used.
The PHI to start with

join:
  %value = phi i32 [ 10, %left ], [ 20, %right ]
  ret i32 %value
Arriving from left selects 10; arriving from right selects 20. A PHI is an SSA merge, not an ordinary instruction that explicitly executes an if statement.
The template to fill in

left:
  ; TODO: store the value associated with the left incoming edge.
  br label %join
right:
  ; TODO: store the value associated with the right incoming edge.
  br label %join
join:
  ; TODO: load the shared slot and return the loaded value.
Step 1 — Allocate one slot in entry
The shared slot must exist before either incoming path uses it. For this simple fixture, one alloca in entry serves both paths.
Step 2 — Replace selection with incoming-path stores

; In left:
store i32 10, ptr %value.slot
; In right:
store i32 20, ptr %value.slot
Only the path chosen by the condition executes. We do not execute both stores every time. In this fixture the stores belong before each predecessor’s branch to join.
Step 3 — Replace the PHI’s use with a load
join loads the slot. The utility replaces the old PHI’s uses and deletes the PHI. Do not access the deleted PHI through a pointer saved in the C++ vector.
The full conceptual result

define i32 @merge(i1 %condition) {
entry:
  %value.slot = alloca i32
  br i1 %condition, label %left, label %right
left:
  store i32 10, ptr %value.slot
  br label %join
right:
  store i32 20, ptr %value.slot
  br label %join
join:
  %value.loaded = load i32, ptr %value.slot
  ret i32 %value.loaded
}
Compare the two utilities

rows: The result computed by that instruction.
The incoming values selected by the executed control-flow path.

blocks.text: Verify

Inspect build/phi-demoted.ll after running the pass with verify. Trace condition=true through left and condition=false through right. The original branch structure should remain at this preparation checkpoint.
Checkpoint: Why does each path load the right value? Why can PHI demotion still leave a new load result used outside its defining block, as in loop.ll?

quiz.q: What replaces the PHI’s incoming-edge selection in the simple diamond?
choices: Both stores always execute and the load chooses one
The taken path executes its store; join reads the slot
The condition is deleted and every path returns zero
quiz.why: Control flow selects which store executes. The load reads the value written on that path.

lessons.title: Assign states before changing edges
lessons.summary: Preserve the real entry as one-time setup and assign deterministic integer IDs to the other original blocks.
lessons.takeaway: Pointer identity is the key; block names are for display.

blocks.text: Task: After both demotion stages, map the original non-entry blocks to unsigned state IDs. Do not create dispatcher blocks during this traversal.
Before you begin — what a state represents

A state number identifies which original block the future dispatcher should run next. It is not an instruction count, a block name, or a new block. In this design, entry stays setup and is excluded from the switch’s ordinary state cases.
The template to start with
Step 1 — Include the map type
#include "llvm/ADT/DenseMap.h"
DenseMap maps a key to a value. Here the key is BasicBlock* and the value is unsigned. The vector keeps the order; the map supports looking up a destination’s ID when rewriting a branch.
Step 2 — Keep setup out of the state loop

if (&BB == entry)
    continue;

The entry block must execute once, particularly its stack allocations. Dispatching through setup repeatedly could allocate storage or repeat initialization on each transition. The pointer returned by &F.getEntryBlock() identifies the actual entry regardless of its name.
Step 3 — Record a block and its ID
Take the address because BB is a reference to the block. The next lesson revisits the pointer and pair-construction errors found in the first draft.
Step 4 — Print in vector order
Iterate stateBlocks to print deterministic output. DenseMap iteration order is not a stable display order. Do not rely on LLVM block names as unique persistent IDs.
The full mapping fragment
Verify

cmake --build build
opt -load-pass-plugin="$PWD/build/libMiniShield.so" \
  -passes='function(minishield-flatten),verify' \
  -disable-output tests/ir/phi.ll
No entry state is assigned. Mapping IDs changes C++ bookkeeping only; it does not itself invalidate analyses. Keep the existing changed decision from demotion.
Checkpoint: Why are a vector and a map both useful? Why does entry not get a state? Why can state zero be an incorrect universal initialization value for a conditional entry?

quiz.q: Why preserve the existing entry as setup?
choices: To avoid reexecuting allocations and initialization on dispatcher iterations
Because LLVM forbids branches in entry
To give it the highest state ID
quiz.why: Setup executes once. The dispatcher routes between the other blocks; entry is not one of its repeated states.

lessons.title: Fix pointer keys and pair insertion
lessons.originalTitle: Fix pointer keys and pair insertion
lessons.summary: Translate the state-map compiler errors into exact C++ types, and distinguish copying a pointer from copying a block.
lessons.takeaway: Use &BB over block objects, but BB over a vector of block pointers.

blocks.text: Task: Review the state-mapping draft and fix its three type/syntax errors before building a dispatcher.
The failing template
Step 1 — Compare addresses

if (entry == &BB)
    continue;
entry is BasicBlock*. BB is BasicBlock&. Comparing entry with &BB compares pointer identity.
Step 2 — Append an address, not an object
stateBlocks.push_back(&BB);
The vector stores BasicBlock*. BB is not already a pointer merely because a reference may be implemented internally using an address.
Step 3 — Use map assignment or a brace-constructed pair

Angle brackets delimit template arguments in DenseMap<...>. Braces construct the key/value pair passed to insert. For this collection every block key is new; bracket assignment is a straightforward choice.
Step 4 — Print the name, not a pointer address
In this loop BB is already a pointer because that is the vector’s element type. lookup receives the pointer key, while -> accesses a block member.
The full corrected loop

Observed error: const auto *BB would be a pointer to const BasicBlock and would not implicitly convert to the map’s BasicBlock* key. const auto BB instead makes the copied pointer itself const. These are different declarations.
Verify

Rebuild and compare the phi.ll state order with lesson 12. lookup returns a default zero for a missing key; in this prototype all original destination blocks must already be mapped, so do not treat lookup as validation that a key exists. Use find() when validating membership.
Checkpoint: Why is copying a pointer element okay here even though for (auto BB : F) would try to copy a noncopyable block?

quiz.q: Which value belongs in a DenseMap<BasicBlock*, unsigned> key?
choices: The block’s address
A copy of the BasicBlock object
The block’s printed name string
quiz.why: The map declaration requires a pointer. Take &BB when iterating block references, and use the pointer directly when iterating stateBlocks.

lessons.title: Construct a complete dispatcher block
lessons.summary: Learn insertion points and IRBuilder while constructing a switch that is deliberately not connected to execution yet.
lessons.takeaway: Every new block needs a terminator, even before it becomes reachable.

blocks.text: Task: After state mapping, add an i32 state slot and two complete new blocks. Preserve the old branch structure at this construction checkpoint.
The template to start with
Step 1 — Choose an insertion point

IRBuilder is a helper for inserting instructions. getFirstInsertionPt() returns an iterator to the first legal insertion position; * obtains the instruction and & takes its address. The builder inserts before that instruction. This expression differs from &*dispatcher, which just recovers a pointer you already had.
Step 2 — Allocate the state once
auto *stateSlot = setup.CreateAlloca(setup.getInt32Ty(), nullptr, "ms.state");

getInt32Ty() returns the LLVM i32 type. CreateAlloca returns the storage pointer. nullptr supplies no array-size operand, meaning the default single element in this overload. The final string is the IR result name. No store is added yet because the dispatcher is deliberately unreachable.
Step 3 — Append the two blocks

LLVMContext owns shared IR context such as uniqued types. &F attaches each block to this function. With no insertion-before argument, the blocks are appended; the original entry remains first. stateBlocks was collected before creation, so neither new block receives a normal state ID.
Step 4 — Terminate the invalid-state path

llvm::IRBuilder<> invalidBuilder(invalidBlock);
invalidBuilder.CreateUnreachable();

unreachable ends the block and declares that this path must never execute in a valid run. It is not a runtime exception handler or a recovery return. Correct state writes must prevent invalid values from selecting it.
Step 5 — Load and switch
CreateLoad needs the loaded value type and pointer. CreateSwitch creates the terminator and sets its default destination. Its third argument reserves case capacity; it does not add case edges.
Step 6 — Populate the cases and mark the mutation

getInt32(ID) creates an i32 integer constant, unlike getInt32Ty(), which supplies a Type*. Keep changed declared before construction so the final preservation result includes the new instructions and blocks.
The full construction stage

Place this after the demotion and state-mapping stages. It replaces the old final preservation return. The variable entry is the BasicBlock* saved during mapping; if your source calls it entry_ptr, use that spelling consistently.
Verify

cmake --build build
opt -load-pass-plugin="$PWD/build/libMiniShield.so" \
  -passes='function(minishield-flatten),verify' \
  -S tests/ir/phi.ll -o build/phi-dispatcher.ll
cat build/phi-dispatcher.ll

Expect a state slot, a dispatcher load and switch with 0→left, 1→right, 2→join, and an invalid block ending in unreachable. ms.dispatch has no predecessors at this checkpoint. Its load is not executed, so no initialization store is needed yet.
Checkpoint: Which block executes the allocation? Why is a switch destination not a substitute for that destination block’s own terminator? Why must new blocks not enter stateBlocks?

choices: No; it reserves capacity, and addCase creates the cases
Yes, it automatically assigns IDs 0, 1, and 2
Only if the function has exactly three blocks
quiz.why: Capacity and contents are separate. Add each integer constant and destination explicitly.

lessons.title: Separate block names from C++ variables
lessons.originalTitle: Separate block names from C++ variables
lessons.summary: Fix the creation errors from the first dispatcher draft and explain exactly why a block pointer is the right return type.
lessons.takeaway: dispatcher is a C++ identifier; "ms.dispatch" is an LLVM name string.

blocks.text: Task: Review the BasicBlock creation statements and the empty invalid block found in the first draft.
The failing template
Step 1 — Use a legal C++ identifier
A dot is member access in C++, not part of an identifier. Writing ms.dispatch makes the parser look for a member named dispatch on an object named ms. Use dispatcher as the variable name.
Step 2 — Keep the returned pointer
BasicBlock::Create returns BasicBlock*. The function owns the attached block. Do not try to construct a local BasicBlock value from that pointer or take the address of an invented local object.
Step 3 — Pass the IR name as a string

auto *dispatcher = llvm::BasicBlock::Create(
    F.getContext(), "ms.dispatch", &F);

The placeholder name in the teaching signature meant “supply a name here”; it was not a predefined variable. Quoted "ms.dispatch" is the block’s display name and may contain a dot even though the C++ identifier cannot.
Step 4 — Finish the invalid block
After the declaration errors are fixed, an empty invalid block would still fail LLVM verification. Compilation checks C++ syntax and types; verify checks the IR your C++ creates.
The full corrected declarations
Observed error: The build failed before producing a new plugin. An existing .so can still contain an older implementation; testing it after a failed build does not verify the draft you just wrote.
Verify
Rebuild successfully, then rerun the phi.ll construction check from lesson 14. Do not proceed merely because an old shared library still loads.
Checkpoint: Distinguish the pointer variable, the object it identifies, and its IR name. Which problem belongs to the C++ compiler and which to the LLVM verifier?

choices: A C++ expression accessing a member
A string naming the LLVM basic block
A pointer to the current dispatcher
quiz.why: The return value is the block pointer. The string argument supplies the IR name.

lessons.title: Connect an unconditional entry branch
lessons.summary: Initialize state from the actual entry successor, insert the replacement instructions, and remove the old branch safely.
lessons.takeaway: Store the selected state before execution reaches the dispatcher.

blocks.text: Task: Connect only an unconditional entry branch first. Use loop.ll, whose entry branches to header, mapped to state 0. This is still a partial transformation.
The template to start with
Step 1 — Save the original terminator

The old branch identifies the real first destination. It also provides an insertion point so replacement instructions can be inserted before it. Keep this code inside the construction block where stateSlot and dispatcher are in scope.
Step 2 — Look up its destination state

auto *destination = entryTerminator->getSuccessor(0);
auto *initialState = entryBuilder.getInt32(stateIDs.lookup(destination));

An unconditional branch has one successor, at index 0. For the loop fixture this is header with ID 0. The lookup must use the destination block, not the entry itself: entry intentionally has no state ID.
Step 3 — Store, branch, then erase

The store runs before the dispatcher’s load. Emit replacements before deleting the old instruction: the builder’s insertion point and the original successor information are still needed. The brief intermediate state with two terminators must not survive to verification. Do not dereference entryTerminator after eraseFromParent().
Step 4 — Leave other entry forms unchanged for now

default: break leaves conditional, switch, return, and unreachable entries untouched at this checkpoint. Do not invent a universal store of zero for them. Later lessons must select the state corresponding to the actual path.
The full entry-rewriting fragment
The full reference file at this checkpoint

This is a complete lib/FlatteningPass.cpp reference to compare after doing the steps. It includes the earlier preparation and mapping, so it replaces the file rather than being appended to your existing run(). It is a study prototype, not a finished production flattener.
Verify

cmake --build build
opt -load-pass-plugin="$PWD/build/libMiniShield.so" \
  -passes='function(minishield-flatten),verify' \
  -S tests/ir/loop.ll -o build/loop-dispatcher.ll
cat build/loop-dispatcher.ll

; Expected entry ending for this fixture:
store i32 0, ptr %ms.state
br label %ms.dispatch

ms.dispatch should now have entry as a predecessor. The original header/body/exit branches are still direct: only the first hop uses the dispatcher. For phi.ll, the conditional entry remains unchanged, so the dispatcher remains unconnected there.

Reference check: this complete example was compiled separately from the learner’s source, passed verify on the 10 existing fixtures, and matched five selected original/transformed lli results (loop counts 4 and 0, both merge paths, and factorial(5)). These are limited checks, not a proof for arbitrary IR or a completed flattener.
What remains after this lesson

items: Handle conditional and switch entries with the correct successor state.
Rewrite original state-block branches to store a new state and return to the dispatcher.
Tighten eligibility for unsupported memory/data-flow cases, including allocations outside the preserved setup block, before treating this as a general transformation.
Use behavior comparisons and regression fixtures in addition to verify. Preserve store-before-load ordering; the switch alone does not prove it.

blocks.text: Checkpoint: Why must the old branch stay alive until replacements are emitted? Why does a conditional entry require more than storing the first state ID?

quiz.q: At this checkpoint, which original branches have been redirected?
choices: Every branch in every function
Only an unconditional entry branch; state-block branches are unchanged
Only return instructions
quiz.why: This connects the first hop. Full flattening needs later successor-selection and state-transition rewriting.

lessons.title: Look up a Day 2 term
lessons.summary: A compact reference for the new SSA, memory, C++ API, and dispatcher vocabulary used in Day 2.
lessons.takeaway: Look up the word, then return to the concrete IR example.

blocks.text: Task: Use this reference when a term interrupts your progress. The Day 1 glossary remains available under the Day 1 tab.
SSA and memory, in one picture
SSA result → store into an entry-allocated slot → load at a use

rows: Static single assignment: each SSA value has one definition; definitions must satisfy dominance requirements at their uses.
A definition’s block lies on every reachable path to a use’s block. New CFG edges can invalidate it.
An SSA merge selecting an incoming value according to the predecessor edge used to enter a block.
Replace selected SSA value flow with stack storage, stores, and loads to prepare for CFG changes.
Storage allocated in the function’s stack frame; the alloca instruction returns a pointer to it.
Read a typed value from memory / write a value to memory. A store has no SSA result.
The instruction produces no value for another instruction to consume, regardless of its operand types.
An instruction result used outside the block in which it was defined. “Escaping” here is not a full escape analysis.
A C++ collection of pointers to instructions to process after discovery; it does not own those instructions.
LLVM type check returning bool / checked cast returning a typed pointer or nullptr.
Treat a derived object as its base type / access a base-typed object through a more specific type after a valid check.
A saved traversal position may stop being valid when its underlying instruction list is changed.
The pass’s report of which cached analysis results remain valid after it runs.
LLVM’s key/value container; here BasicBlock* keys map to unsigned IDs. Iteration order is not presentation order.
The integer naming a destination block in our dispatcher; not the same as the block’s optional printed name.
A block loading the next state and switching to the corresponding original block.
The preserved one-time function entry, holding allocations and initialization outside repeated state dispatch.
LLVM’s shared context for IR facilities such as uniqued types; obtained here from the function.
An LLVM helper that inserts instructions at a chosen position or at the end of a block.
The position where the builder will insert the next instruction; a pointer-based constructor can insert before an existing instruction.
Get the LLVM i32 Type / get an i32 ConstantInt holding a particular value.
Reserved space is not an edge. addCase associates an integer constant with a destination block.
The final instruction in a complete basic block; replacements must leave exactly one valid terminator.
A terminator declaring that the path must not execute in a valid run; it is not recovery logic.
Remove and delete an instruction from its block. Do not use its pointer afterward.
A deliberately limited stage that can verify without implementing all supported input cases or full flattening.

quiz.q: Which pair denotes a type and a value, respectively?
choices: getInt32Ty() and getInt32(2)
getInt32(2) and getInt32Ty()
eraseFromParent() and continue
quiz.why: An instruction builder often needs both an LLVM Type* and particular constant values. They are different API inputs.
